::: {.quest-dialog}
**Prerequisites:** Save Point, a laptop with about 16 GB of memory, a terminal, and roughly 5 GB of free disk. This is an optional side quest. WSL (Windows Subsystem for Linux) users: see the unconfirmed list at the end.
**Objective:** run a small local model with Ollama, give it enough context, and point OpenCode at it.
**Time:** about 20 minutes. Everything stays on your machine.

## The Pet

A small local model is gentle, free, and private. It also forgets things quickly and gets things wrong more often than a large hosted model. That is fine if you know it.

## 1. Install Ollama and fetch a model

```bash
curl -fsSL https://ollama.com/install.sh | sh     # macOS and Linux
ollama pull qwen3:4b                              # about 2.5 GB
ollama run qwen3:4b "Say hello in one sentence."
```

`qwen3:4b` is one example of a small model that Ollama lists with tool support. Model names change quickly, so check the "tools" badge on the model's page at ollama.com/library. The docs make no promise that a model fits your RAM (ordinary memory), so test it: `ollama ps` shows what loaded while it runs.

## 2. Give it room to think

Ollama's docs say the default context (the context length, which is the same thing as the context window: how much text the model can see at once) is **4k tokens** on machines with under 24 GiB of video memory (VRAM, the memory on the graphics card or shared with it), which includes a 16 GB laptop. Agents and coding tools need **at least 64k**, and OpenCode says it requires 64k or higher. Set it when you start the server:

```bash
OLLAMA_CONTEXT_LENGTH=64000 ollama serve
```

Check what loaded with `ollama ps`. A bigger context needs more memory and can push work onto the CPU (the main processor; graphics hardware is faster), which is slow, so the Pet may be a patient companion.

## 3. Point OpenCode at it

Install OpenCode (the official docs currently give this command), then connect inside it with `/connect` (a `/command` is typed inside the running tool):

```bash
curl -fsSL https://opencode.ai/v2/install | bash
```

OpenCode finds Ollama at `http://127.0.0.1:11434` automatically. To spell it out, put this in `~/.config/opencode/opencode.json`:

```json
{
  "$schema": "https://opencode.ai/config.json",
  "providers": {
    "ollama": { "settings": { "baseURL": "http://127.0.0.1:11434/v1" } }
  }
}
```

## Other small models to try

Qwen is one family among several. Mistral publishes open-weight models that Ollama lists with tool support: `ministral-3` comes in 3B (3.0 GB), 8B (6.0 GB) and 14B (9.1 GB) sizes under Apache 2.0, and `mistral-small` is 24B (14 GB). Sizes and licences: Last verified (docs, not run) on 2026-11-20; sources in `research/mistral.md`. A 24B model needs far more memory than a 3B one, so check `ollama ps` after loading. We ran `ministral-3:8b` (not through OpenCode) for chat in [Grow a Graph with Ollama](../codon-mill/grow-a-graph-with-ollama.html), where it gave valid JSON but misread a note. Not checked: how `ministral-3` behaves as an OpenCode backend. Mistral also has its own open-source terminal agent, Mistral Vibe; see [Pick Your Companion](pick-your-companion.html).

## 4. Put the Pet on a leash

OpenCode's default policy is **allow everything** (except reading `.env` files, which it asks about). The docs also warn: *"Shell is not a sandbox. It runs with the host user's authority."* Each rule says `allow` (run without asking), `ask` (prompt you first) or `deny` (never run). A safer start asks about everything first, then narrows. **Rules are checked in order and the last match wins:**

```json
{
  "permissions": [
    { "action": "*", "resource": "*", "effect": "ask" },
    { "action": "shell", "resource": "git status *", "effect": "allow" },
    { "action": "shell", "resource": "git push *", "effect": "deny" }
  ]
}
```

Free hosted models are a different thing from the Pet: someone else runs them. See the optional quest [Free Is Not Free](free-is-not-free.html) before you send them anything.

## Unconfirmed (check before relying on it)

- WSL: neither Ollama nor OpenCode publishes WSL guidance. Installing both inside your WSL distro is our best guess, and no vendor documents it.
- OpenCode is in a version change: its pages differ on some config keys, so if a snippet errors, check the current docs.
- Small models are more error-prone than large ones. That comes from common experience, and the vendors do not document it.

## A built-in Pet on newer Macs

If you use a recent Mac, Apple ships its own small on-device model with the operating system, and developers can call it through Apple's Foundation Models framework. Apple's updates page mentions macOS 27 changing the model (June 2026) and a Python SDK for it (March 2026). Availability depends on whether your device and region support Apple Intelligence, and the model can take a while to download after you turn that on. Apple's documentation says it suits summarising, extracting and classifying text, and that it may struggle with basic math, code and logical reasoning, which is a helpful guide to what to ask of any small local model.

Not checked: whether OpenCode, Claude Code or any other coding agent can use this model as its backend. The pages read describe the framework for app developers and do not mention coding agents. It is a fun thing to try if you are curious, and nothing on this site depends on it.

## Lore

*Further reading. Optional.*

- [ministral-3](https://ollama.com/library/ministral-3): Ollama library, docs. Why read: it lists the sizes, context length, tool support and licence of a small Mistral model you can pull instead of a Qwen one.
- [OpenCode](https://docs.ollama.com/integrations/opencode): Ollama, docs. Why read: it is the vendor guide to running OpenCode against a local Ollama model, including the context length it needs. It still shows older OpenCode install commands, so check the OpenCode docs too.
- [Providers](https://opencode.ai/docs/providers/): OpenCode, docs. Why read: it shows how to connect Ollama or an OpenAI-compatible gateway in the current config format.
- [Config](https://opencode.ai/docs/config/): OpenCode, docs. Why read: it lists where `opencode.json` lives and how global and project files override each other.
- [Permissions](https://opencode.ai/docs/permissions/): OpenCode, docs. Why read: it explains how to control what the agent may do, which matters more with a small local model.
- [Foundation Models updates](https://developer.apple.com/documentation/updates/foundationmodels): Apple, docs. Why read: it lists the changes to Apple's on-device model by date, including which OS versions change the model.
- [anomalyco/opencode](https://github.com/anomalyco/opencode): GitHub, repo. Why read: it is the source and release list, useful when the docs and your installed version disagree.
:::
